title: U.S. Defense Boss Asks Asian Allies to Spend More on Military
summary: Imagine a huge meeting where top military leaders from all over Asia gather to talk about keeping the region safe. That's the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore, and this year, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had a clear message for America's allies: spend more money on your militaries. Why? He says China is building up its military in a big way, and that worries many countries. Hegseth said U.S.-China relations are 'better than they've been in many years,' especially after President Trump met with China's leader Xi Jinping recently. But he also said there is 'rightful alarm' about China's military activities. Here's what got people talking: Hegseth didn't mention Taiwan in his speech. Taiwan is a self-governing island that China claims as its own, and last year Hegseth spoke strongly about China harassing Taiwan. This time, he skipped it. When someone in the audience asked about Taiwan, he said the U.S. has enough weapons and that future arms sales are up to President Trump. Some experts were disappointed. Ankit Panda, a nuclear policy expert who was listening, said the speech was 'really light on substance'—meaning it didn't have many details or clear plans. Vietnam's president spoke earlier and warned that 'unchecked competition' between big powers is risky. Smaller countries often feel stuck between the U.S. and China. China didn't send its defense minister for the second year in a row, sending lower-level experts instead. One Chinese expert said Hegseth's speech was more moderate than last year's. The big question remains: how can the U.S. and China avoid conflict while competing for influence?
why_it_matters: This shows how world leaders try to prevent fights through meetings and alliances, much like how you would talk things out with friends to avoid a big argument.

background_read: The Shangri-La Dialogue is a yearly security meeting in Singapore where ministers from many countries talk about keeping the Asia-Pacific region peaceful.
The United States has several allies in Asia, like Japan, South Korea, and the Philippines, who work together to prevent conflicts.
Taiwan is a self-governing island that China claims as its own territory, which often creates tension between China and other countries.
President Donald Trump (the U.S. president since 2025) has tried to keep a mix of talking and showing strength when dealing with China.
Article_Structure: WHO: U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, military leaders from Asian allies, and expert Ankit Panda
WHAT: Hegseth urged allies to increase military spending because of China's growing armed forces, but he avoided mentioning Taiwan in his speech
WHERE: The Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore
WHY: The U.S. is worried about China's military expansion and wants allies to share more of the responsibility for keeping the region safe

perspectives.description: A stronger group of allies can make everyone safer by discouraging any one country from starting a war.
Leaving out Taiwan might have confused or upset some allies, and the speech lacked clear plans for how to handle China's growing power.
Smaller countries often feel stuck between the U.S. and China, trying to stay friends with both while protecting their own interests.
